Area.evidence_source: Analysis of the interviews indicated that the strongest protective factors were linked to existential issues whereby the  participants felt a sense of purpose and competence in their  life roles. In the comparative analysis between the repeated attempters and nonattempters (Table 2), there was no  significant difference in the report of having responsibilities for children and religious practice, two variables that  are commonly perceived as suicide protective factors. In  the interview sample, these variables as protective factors  were tenuous when the participants were decompensating  from their mental illness. Among the five female participants who had children, there was a deep sense of guilt  and shame that they could not care for them, and that their  children would be better off with their extended family.  One participant believed that killing herself was a suitable  option to provide for her son who was a beneficiary of her  life insurance policy. Of the two participants who were practicing the Christian faith at the time of their suicide attempts, they heard  voices reprimanding them for their sins and urging them  to kill themselves. However, the role of these variables  as protective factors strengthened when the same participants experienced a sense of psychological well-being and  found more comfort in their faith. A comparative analysis on the protective role of existential issues was also made between six participants in  the interview sample who showed some reported improvement in their clinical symptoms and treatment adherence  and the other participants who did not make any progress  in their recovery. It appeared that these participants' recovery progress was closely related to a more positive outlook  about their lives that was missing among the other participants. There were two interrelated themes that spoke to  this glimmer of hope and optimism as well as motivation  to remain in treatment among the six participants.
